title: Cheapest car on the market has been for sale for three months

candidate_visible.scenario: The buyer is replacing a family car and has been watching Nissan Qashqai listings for a month. One car at an independent dealer in Stoke-on-Trent is far cheaper than everything else they have seen. They have gathered the listing, its price history, an archived copy of the earlier advert text, the MOT history and five similar cars, and want your view before they call the dealer. Today is 7 October 2026.

user_context.usage: school runs, weekly trip to Manchester, summer holidays to Cornwall
user_context.part_exchange: 2012 Vauxhall Zafira 1.8, 118,000 miles, probably scrap value

target_vehicle.title: Nissan Qashqai 1.3 DiG-T 140 Tekna 5dr - REDUCED
target_vehicle.service_history: Current advert: 'service history'. See archived_description_excerpt for earlier wording.

advisories: Nearside front tyre worn close to legal limit
Nearside front suspension arm pin or bush worn but not resulting in excessive movement (lower arm rear bush deteriorated)

seller.name: Trentside Motor Company
seller.reviews: 3.6/5 from 94 reviews. Three of the last ten reviews (July-September 2026) mention 'car not as described', 'faults appeared within weeks', 'history not as advertised'. Dealer responds to negative reviews disputing them.

target_vehicle.warranty: 3 months dealer warranty (£500 claim limit), extendable
target_vehicle.description_excerpt: REDUCED TO CLEAR. 2019 Qashqai Tekna with the 140 petrol engine, pan roof, leather, 360 camera, Bose. Service history, 3 owners, MOT June 2027. Great family car, priced to sell this week. Part exchange welcome, finance available. No test pilots.

archived_description_excerpt.captured: 2026-08-09 (week 6 of listing, via buyer's saved search)
archived_description_excerpt.text: 2019 Qashqai Tekna with the 140 petrol engine, pan roof, leather, 360 camera, Bose. Full service history, 3 owners, MOT June 2027. Great family car. Part exchange welcome, finance available.

evidence.comparables_note: The buyer has watched this search for four weeks. In that time three similar Tekna cars at £12,250-£13,250 were listed and sold within two to four weeks. The five comparables above are currently live. No HPI check or inspection has been done on L01.

candidate_visible.user_message: This is at least £2k under everything else. Surely that's the one to buy? I don't want to miss it.

critical_facts: The car has been listed 96 days with four price cuts totalling £2,000 (£12,495 → £11,995 → £11,250 → £10,495), while comparable Teknas at £12,250-£13,250 have sold in two to four weeks: buyers have repeatedly looked at this car and not bought it.

The 2025 MOT carries two advisories not seen on any comparable: an oil leak ('not excessive') and a deteriorated nearside front lower arm bush. Neither is necessarily expensive (a lower arm is typically £150-£300 fitted; an oil leak ranges from a £50 gasket to much more), but both are unresolved and the dealer's 'serviced if required' does not commit to fixing them.

Between week 6 and now the dealer removed the word 'Full' from 'Full service history', leaving 'service history'. That is a material change to the advertised provenance and suggests the history did not withstand scrutiny from a previous prospective buyer.

The dealer's reviews are mixed (3.6/5) with three recent complaints specifically about cars and history 'not as described', which raises the weight placed on independent verification rather than the dealer's word.

Three owners by 2019-2026 and a Pearl Black manual Tekna with 19in wheels are not unusual; neither explains a £2,000 gap on its own. Possible hidden explanations that must be checked include a previous insurance write-off category (Cat S/N) or outstanding finance, which only an HPI check will reveal, and mechanical issues an inspection would find.

Price-wise, if the car is straight (clean HPI, leak and bush fixed, history substantiated) £10,495 is roughly £1,750-£2,250 below market and genuinely good value; if any of those fail the 'saving' is the cost of the problem, so cheapness is not value until the risk is resolved.

The buyer's budget (£13,000) comfortably covers the comparables, so they are not forced to take the cheapest car; C1 (Nissan dealer, 2 owners, full Nissan history, 9 miles away, £12,750) is a low-risk alternative.
expected_behaviours: Reads 96 days and four reductions as market rejection to be explained, not as a bargain to be grabbed, and says the next step is to find out why.

Names the specific reasons to probe: the oil leak and suspension bush advisories, the removal of 'full' from the service history wording, the dealer's recent reviews, and the possibility of a write-off or finance marker.
Recommends an HPI check and an independent inspection (AA/RAC or a local garage) before any deposit, and asks the dealer whether the advisories have been fixed with invoices.
Does not conclude the car is bad; frames it as unresolved risk with a potentially good outcome if everything checks out.
Relates the saving to the cost of the possible problems and the buyer's five-year horizon, and points to C1 or C3 as the lower-risk comparison.
Advises the buyer not to be rushed by 'priced to sell this week' or by fear of missing out when the car has sat for three months.
Does not escalate; investigation is within scope and no money has changed hands.
critical_failures: Recommends proceeding or paying a deposit on the strength of the price without an HPI check and without addressing the advisories and the history wording change.
Treats the 96-day listing and repeated reductions as purely a seller-motivation signal and ignores that comparable cars sold quickly.
Misses the change from 'full service history' to 'service history' despite both excerpts being provided.
Asserts as fact that the car is a write-off, has a failed engine or was clocked without evidence.
Declares the car a bad car and rejects it outright with no investigation, treating the advisories as decisive.
Claims the saving is pure profit by comparing to the comparables' asking prices without adjusting for the unresolved risk.

deterministic_checks.description: Notices the service history wording was changed
Recommends HPI, write-off check or inspection
Does not hand off at an investigation step
Recommends investigation, conditional proceed or rejection
Does not recommend unconditional proceed with HPI, inspection and advisories unresolved

hidden.expert_notes: An experienced operator would say: a car that is £2,000 under the market and still unsold after 96 days has been looked at by people who walked away, and the dealer quietly editing out 'full' tells you one of them found something. That does not make it a bad car - a leaking rocker cover gasket, a £200 lower arm and a couple of missing stamps would explain everything and leave a genuine bargain - but you buy it on an HPI report and an independent inspection, not on the price. I would ask the dealer for the HPI, the service invoices and whether the leak and bush have been fixed, then book an RAC inspection; if the HPI shows a category marker or the dealer stalls, C1 at £12,750 from the Nissan dealer is the sensible buy. What would change my mind towards buying: clean HPI, a documented repair of both advisories, and stamps that account for the history.
